revisions.body: Once heavy drinking is ruled out, Eryximachus gives the evening a new engine: he replaces the just-arrived flute-girl’s performance with speeches among the men and takes charge of the next procedure. The point is not merely that talk begins. I read this change of medium as a rescue of the gathering from drift: bodily exhaustion becomes the reason to organize attention.

The close turns incompletion into a handoff. Eryximachus admits that his praise may leave things out, then gives Aristophanes a choice: complete it or praise Eros another way. Hear the recovered hiccup as a comic reminder that this next speech arrives through the bodily interruption that reordered the speaking turns.
A compact contrast: Gorgias uses medicine analogically for correcting the soul, whereas Eryximachus defines it through the body's erotic regulation.

crossrefs.note: medicine as analogy for the soul's correction, against medicine as the body's erotic science

revisions.body: Does Eryximachus's final promise of happiness and friendship with the gods follow from the forms of erotic regulation he has described, or merely repeat his governing analogy?

Rather than continue in his own voice, Socrates introduces Diotima of Mantinea, whom he presents as his teacher in erotic matters. He says that, in his earlier exchange with her, he had spoken in much the same terms as Agathon had just used, and that she refuted him with the arguments he has now used against Agathon. The scene invites us to hear the exchange as a deliberate re-performance, while the speech that follows remains Diotima’s teaching reported within Socrates’ speech.

The appearance of Alcestis and Achilles makes this passage sound like a return to the evening’s heroic examples. Here, however, Diotima places their deaths beside Codrus’s within an argument about the immortal memory of virtue. One way to hear the move is as a reframing rather than a correction: the heroic actions now serve as examples for Diotima’s claim that human striving reaches toward immortal virtue and renown.

Socrates now steps out of Diotima’s reported speech: he says he is persuaded and seeks to persuade others that Love is the best helper for the human possession at issue. He does not merely report that conviction; he urges everyone to honor Love, says he practices erotic matters, and praises Love’s power and valor. If this is offered as an encomium, what kind of praise is it—an argument, a personal profession, or both?

Alcibiades presents two kinds of scene. His account of the night beside Socrates ends in a familial comparison rather than erotic intimacy, and he claims personal access to Socrates’s inner images. The campaign episodes widen the setting: soldiers notice the barefoot walk on ice, some Ionians keep watch through the night, and at Delium Alcibiades meets Socrates retreating with Laches. The contrast matters less as independent corroboration than as a change in scale: private testimony becomes a series of scenes observed within military life.

Alcibiades does not say that every great man has an exact double. He grants that some features of other figures can be matched: Achilles with Brasidas and others, Pericles with Nestor and Antenor, with further examples possible. Socrates is then presented as unlike any human, ancient or present; only as a possible exception does Alcibiades suggest the Silenuses and satyrs, for Socrates and his speeches alike. The climax turns praise into a problem of comparison: what image could name a singularity?
